Yes. Diving in Japan runs from warm coral reefs in Okinawa, with manta rays and turtles, to cool kelp and macro life off the Izu Peninsula near Tokyo. The south is best from late spring to autumn. Bring proof of certification, and book an operator that offers English briefings.

Okinawa is where most diving in Japan begins, and rightly so. The water stays warm from spring through autumn, and visibility regularly passes 100 feet (30 meters). The Blue Cave at Cape Maeda is the signature site on the main island. It is a half-submerged sea cave, and light through its underwater mouth turns the interior a deep sapphire. It suits snorkelers and certified divers alike.
The Kerama reefs, protected as a national park since 2014.

In winter, the same waters draw schooling hammerhead sharks. That is a separate trip for advanced divers only, in colder and rougher seas. Operators are selective about whom they take. Booked well, it is among the rarest sights in Japanese waters: dozens of hammerheads passing through deep blue at the country’s western edge.
Winter hammerheads at Yonaguni, the most demanding dive in Japan.

For the same reason, Izu is popular with Tokyo divers on a spare weekend. The water demands more thermal protection, which shapes what you pack. Many visitors also pair a day of diving here with a night at a hot-spring inn on the peninsula.

Take the warm-water giants first. The whale shark is the largest fish in the ocean, yet it is harmless and feeds on plankton. Similarly, the reefs hold their color well. The Kerama gardens stay healthy under national-park protection.

Fish life fills out the picture. Expect schooling jacks, parrotfish, orange anthias clouding the coral heads and the occasional reef shark. Clownfish sit in their anemones, lionfish hang under ledges, and cuttlefish drift along the sand. Together, they make a typical southern dive feel crowded with life.

Season is the single decision that shapes scuba diving in Japan, and it works differently in each region. In Okinawa and the southern islands, the prime window runs from late spring through autumn. Water sits in the low to mid 80s Fahrenheit through summer and eases into the high 70s by late autumn. Summer also brings the manta season at Ishigaki.

Summer brings typhoons, too, and they can cancel boat days at short notice. For that reason, late spring and early autumn are the wiser choice. The water is warm enough and clear enough, and the seas are usually calmer. Even at the height of summer, a thin wetsuit is worth wearing against coral and sun.

For mainland and shoulder-season diving where the water turns truly cool, a full 5mm wetsuit is essential. A well-fitted suit from a serious maker, such as the Fourth Element Proteus II, adds weeks each year to the Izu season. Most operators rent suits, but a borrowed suit rarely fits well.

Beyond that, certification is expected, and at Yonaguni advanced certification and logged experience are genuinely required. First, dive insurance such as a DAN membership costs little against the price of a chamber treatment. Second, nitrox is widely available at the larger Okinawa operators for certified divers.

The deeper question is how to combine diving in Japan with the rest of the country. Few people fly across the Pacific only to dive. Instead, a well-built trip threads a few days underwater in the south with the cities, the food and the mountains on the mainland. Our guide to

One practical rule matters more than the rest. Leave 18 to 24 hours between your last dive and any flight, as dive-safety guidelines advise. In practice, a final dive day in Okinawa should end with a slow evening and a good dinner. It should never end with a dash to Naha airport.

A mask that seals is the difference between a dive and an ordeal. Rental masks are fitted to an average face, and many faces are not average. Of all the gear in this list, the mask is the piece most worth fitting to your own face. Premium models such as the Atomic Aquatics Venom use Schott glass and a soft dual-density skirt for a gentle seal.

Okinawa’s reefs are fragile and increasingly protected, and the local diving community takes conservation seriously. The most useful thing anyone diving in Japan can do is keep chemical sunscreen out of the water. Two common filters, oxybenzone and octinoxate, are linked by

Good habits matter as much as the right sunscreen. Hold neutral buoyancy, keep your fins clear of the coral and take only photographs. At current-prone sites like Yonaguni, a surface marker buoy is genuine safety equipment rather than a courtesy. Deploy it before you ascend, not after, and the boat finds you rather than the other way around.

General info about Japan & diving there
Because Japan is an archipelagic country with islands covering over 1800 miles (3,000km), there is a huge difference in water temperature between north and south.

Northern Japan (Hokkaido) tends to be cool or cold. Southern Japan (Kyushu and Okinawa) consists of hundreds of islands and islets in the very deep south of the Japanese archipelago. It’s warm year-round with temperatures around 68°F (20°C) in winter and 88°F (31°C) during the summer, making it ideal for crystal clear waters, white sand, and colorful fish.

Japan is also volcanic with a fascinating underwater topography such as steep vertical walls and interesting rock formations. A lot of the islands in southern Japan and south of the capital Tokyo were formed from volcanic eruptions, and as dive guides will explain, this is plain to see when you go diving.

The Kuroshio Current also flows northward on the Pacific side of Japan and warms the seas as far north as Tokyo, usually around May.

After a 12-hour journey south of Tokyo on the overnight ferry, a tiny mountain appears in the distance that looks very much like a mini Mt Fuji. This is Hachijojima, a quaint little volcanic island with black sandy beaches, warm water, and diverse marine life.

Turtles are often spotted but the fish to look for is the Yuzen or Wrought Iron Butterfly Fish. Because they’re endemic to Japan, seeing these metallic black and white species is a very special moment.

In Japan, it’s more of a taster than an actual dive but it’s one of the most challenging and unusual opportunities divers like to take. There may not be much to the sites but you can see a few fish, sea urchins, starfish, and shrimp.
